items.title: Serum IL-33/sST2 is associated with polymyositis/dermatomyositis complicated with interstitial lung disease.
items.abstract: To investigate serum levels of interleukin-33 (IL-33) and soluble ST2 (sST2) in patients with polymyositis/dermatomyositis (PM/DM), and analyze their correlation with clinical indicators. Serum IL-33, sST2, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) marker cell-free DNA (cfDNA) were measured in 60 PM/DM patients and 20 healthy controls. The correlations between these indicators and their relationships with clinical data were analyzed. IL-33 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) was detected by Western blot, and its effect on NETs formation was observed via high-content live-cell imaging. PM/DM patients showed significantly elevated serum IL-33, sST2, and cfDNA levels compared with controls (all p < 0.01). ELISA-detected serum IL-33 levels showed no significant difference between PM/DM patients with and without ILD, while Western blot analysis revealed significantly higher IL-33 protein expression in PBMCs from the ILD group than from the non-ILD group. Of note, IL-33 expression at the cellular (PBMCs) level, but not serum IL-33, was associated with ILD in PM/DM patients. sST2 levels were also higher in PM/DM patients with ILD. IL-33 induced NETs formation in neutrophils. IL-33 and sST2 levels positively correlated with cfDNA and lung CT scores in PM/DM-ILD patients. Multiple linear regression identified IL-33, sST2, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) as independent factors for cfDNA. ROC analysis showed that the combination of sST2, ESR, and CRP yielded an AUC of 0.911 for diagnosing ILD, which was superior to any single indicator. Elevated IL-33 and sST2 in PM/DM correlate with inflammation, muscle injury, ILD, and NETs formation, suggesting the IL-33/ST2 pathway may contribute to PM/DM-ILD pathogenesis by promoting NETs formation. Key Points • Serum IL-33 and sST2 levels are significantly elevated in PM/DM patients, and correlate with inflammation, muscle injury, and disease activity. • IL-33 promotes NETs formation in neutrophils, and serum cfDNA positively correlates with IL-33 and sST2, suggesting the IL-33/ST2 axis may contribute to PM/DM-ILD pathogenesis through inducing NETs. • sST2 has discriminative value for ILD in PM/DM, and its combination with ESR and CRP improves diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.911), supporting its potential as a clinical biomarker panel.

items.title: Choroidal changes in psoriatic arthritis assessed by optical coherence tomography: a cross-sectional study.
items.abstract: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disorder with diverse musculoskeletal and systemic manifestations. While ocular involvement most often presents as uveitis, subclinical choroidal changes remain underexplored. The choroidal vascularity index (CVI), which is considered less influenced by physiologic variability than choroidal thickness (CT), has not yet been comprehensively evaluated in PsA. This study aimed to investigate CT and CVI in patients with PsA compared with healthy controls. In this cross-sectional study, optical coherence tomography (OCT) with enhanced depth imaging was performed to measure CT at subfoveal, nasal, and temporal points, and CVI was calculated using ImageJ software. Clinical data, including disease activity indices, laboratory markers, and psoriasis-related clinical scores, were recorded. Forty-five PsA patients fulfilling the CASPAR criteria and 45 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were included. CVI was significantly lower in PsA patients compared with controls (60.88 ± 3.82 vs. 66.76 ± 3.81; p < 0.001). Although CT values tended to be higher in PsA patients, only selected measurements remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. In univariate regression analysis, axial involvement was associated with lower CVI values (B =  - 2.39, p = 0.046), while increasing age showed a borderline positive association with CVI (B = 0.112, p = 0.064). In multivariable analysis adjusted for age and BMI, axial involvement remained independently associated with lower CVI (B =  - 2.656, p = 0.025); however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the limited subgroup size. Patients with PsA demonstrated lower CVI compared with healthy controls, suggesting the presence of subclinical choroidal microvascular alterations. CVI may provide additional insight beyond conventional CT measurements in the assessment of ocular involvement in PsA.

items.title: Design and optimization of a nano‑transethosomes gel for dual delivery of diclofenac sodium and luteolin using a Box-Behnken approach for enhanced rheumatoid arthritis therapy.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis involves chronic autoimmune-driven synovial inflammation, oxidative stress, and joint degeneration. Luteolin (L) and diclofenac sodium (D) offer complementary anti-inflammatory effects, though each has limitations related to bioavailability or long-term safety. This study aimed to develop and optimise a transethosomal gel for the topical co-delivery of luteolin and diclofenac sodium to enhance dermal permeation and therapeutic efficacy. The formulation was optimised using an experimental design approach based on vesicle size, PDI, and entrapment efficiency. The optimised formulation (LD-TE-Opt) was incorporated into Carbopol 934-based gel and evaluated for physicochemical characteristics, in vitro drug release, ex vivo skin permeation, and pharmacological activity. The optimized system was incorporated into a gel and evaluated through physicochemical characterization along with in vitro and in vivo anti-arthritic assessments. Prepared transethosomes formulation presented vesicles size of 77.99 ± 0.62 nm, zeta potential - 38.3 mV, polydispersity index 0.2618 ± 0.002, entrapment efficiency of 80.44 ± 0.12% for luteolin, 76.37 ± 0.32% for diclofenac sodium, and in vitro release profiling of LD-TE-Opt was cumulative drug release: 85.04 ± 3.53% over 24 h. The optimized LD-TE-Opt formulation exhibited significant anti-arthritic activity, demonstrating greater efficacy than the diclofenac sodium. The LD-TE-OptG formulation demonstrated a thermal response time of 20.03 ± 0.15 s, indicating good analgesic activity. Further, LD-TE-OptG effectively reduced paw volume to 3.41 ± 0.03 mL by day 28, demonstrating significant anti-arthritic activity compared to the control and CFA-induced group. Luteolin-diclofenac co‑delivery produced a combined therapeutic effect anti‑arthritic response with limited toxicity, positioning the dual‑drug nanoformulation as a promising therapeutic horizon for rheumatoid arthritis.

items.title: A Hidden Cause of Aspiration Pneumonia: Anti-HMG-CoA Reductase Immune-mediated Necrotizing Myopathy.
items.abstract: Anti-HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR)-positive immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) typically presents with marked creatine kinase (CK) elevation and progressive proximal limb weakness, but atypical presentations can delay diagnosis. We report an 85-year-old man taking atorvastatin who presented with three days of progressive dysphagia and fever and was found to have aspiration pneumonia with marked CK elevation. Manual muscle testing showed mild weakness of neck flexion, right elbow flexion, and bilateral knee extension. Bedside swallowing assessment demonstrated impairment, and videofluoroscopic swallowing study confirmed post-swallow aspiration. Magnetic Resonance Imaging showed hyperintense signal changes in the quadriceps muscles of both thighs. Anti-HMGCR antibodies were positive, and muscle biopsy demonstrated scattered necrotic and regenerating myofibers with minimal inflammatory infiltrates, consistent with IMNM. Atorvastatin was discontinued and immunotherapy initiated, including intravenous immunoglobulin followed by high-dose glucocorticoids. Rituximab was added as escalation therapy because of high disease activity and difficulty continuing oral immunosuppressive therapy due to dysphagia. CK declined and subsequently normalized, and dysphagia clinically improved. Anti-HMGCR IMNM should be considered in statin-exposed elderly patients presenting with subacute dysphagia or aspiration pneumonia and unexplained hyperCKemia, even when limb weakness is subtle.

items.title: Severe Progressive Interstitial Lung Disease in Seronegative Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is a subtype of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by severe proximal weakness and myofiber necrosis with minimal inflammation. Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is uncommon in IMNM, particularly in seronegative cases, with limited published data on its clinical features. We present a 72-year-old man, a lifelong never-smoker, with previously diagnosed "idiopathic" ILD who presented with acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Despite negative myositis-specific antibodies and normal creatine kinase (CK), mildly elevated aldolase and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings prompted muscle biopsy, which confirmed IMNM. He was treated with combination immunosuppression including corticosteroids, mycophenolate, rituximab, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), with significant improvement in respiratory and muscle function at six months and sustained respiratory and muscle function through 14-18 months of follow-up. This case demonstrates that seronegative IMNM can present with severe, progressive ILD. Normal CK should not exclude the diagnosis, particularly when muscle atrophy is present. Aldolase elevation and muscle biopsy are essential diagnostic tools in seronegative cases.

items.title: Improvement of refractory cognitive impairment following anifrolumab treatment in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus.
items.abstract: Anifrolumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting the type I interferon receptor, has been approved for the treatment of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). However, its role in cognitive impairment remains unclear. A woman in her early 70s was diagnosed with SLE based on the presence of pancytopenia, proteinuria, hypocomplementemia, and elevated serum anti-double-stranded DNA antibody levels. Treatment was initiated with oral prednisolone at 50 mg/day and intravenous cyclophosphamide at 500 mg. Cognitive dysfunction persisted despite improvements in systemic manifestations, with a decreased Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score and abnormalities on the clock drawing test (CDT). Results from brain magnetic resonance imaging were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed mildly elevated interleukin-6 levels, but negative results for anti-ribosomal P antibodies. Although delirium was initially considered among the differential diagnoses, the patient did not meet the criteria for delirium. Cognitive impairment associated with SLE disease activity was therefore suspected. A second infusion of cyclophosphamide was administered, but cognitive impairment exacerbated. Intravenous infusion of anifrolumab was subsequently initiated, after which cognitive function improved over several days, with increasing MMSE score and normalization of CDT performance. No relapse of SLE was seen with anifrolumab every four weeks combined with hydroxychloroquine, and prednisolone was tapered to 4 mg/day by 11 months after treatment initiation. Although the relative contributions of neuropsychiatric involvement and excessive type I interferon activity to cognitive impairment remain uncertain, this case raises the possibility that anifrolumab may have contributed to the improvement of cognitive impairment.

items.title: When Hip Pain Is Vascular: Internal Iliac Artery Aneurysmal Lesion in Behçet's Disease Treated with a Covered Stent.
items.abstract: Behçet's disease is a chronic relapsing systemic vasculitis in which arterial involvement is less common than venous disease but carries substantial rupture risk. Internal iliac artery involvement is rare and may be overlooked because symptoms are often nonspecific. We report a 34-year-old man with established Behçet's disease referred from orthopaedic surgery after 2 to 3 months of right hip and deep gluteal pain initially considered musculoskeletal. Plain hip x-ray was unremarkable. Pelvic imaging demonstrated a right pelvic arterial lesion, and computed tomography angiography (CTA) confirmed a 57 mm saccular aneurysmal lesion arising from the right internal iliac artery. Inflammatory markers were elevated, and perioperative immunosuppression was optimized with rheumatology input. Endovascular repair was performed via contralateral left common femoral access using a 6 × 60 mm self-expanding covered stent graft across the diseased internal iliac segment, without adjunctive coil embolization. Completion angiography showed complete sac exclusion with preserved distal internal iliac flow. Recovery was uneventful. One-month CTA confirmed persistent exclusion and stent-graft patency, and the patient remained clinically asymptomatic at 12 months. This case highlights an orthopaedic mimic and supports carefully selected flow-preserving endovascular repair under immunosuppressive cover, with lifelong imaging surveillance to detect late complications in this inflammatory disease setting.Clinical ImpactInternal iliac artery aneurysmal lesions are rare manifestations of vascular Behçet's disease and may present with hip, buttock or groin pain due to deep pelvic mass effect, leading to initial orthopaedic referral and potential diagnostic delay. This case emphasizes the need to consider a vascular cause in Behçet's disease patients with unexplained persistent pelvic or hip pain, especially when plain radiographs are normal. It also illustrates a flow-preserving endovascular strategy using a covered stent graft to exclude the lesion while maintaining internal iliac artery patency. Because Behçet's disease is an inflammatory vasculitis, technical success alone is insufficient; perioperative immunosuppression and lifelong clinical and imaging surveillance remain central to management.

items.title: Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug (DMARD) use and associated survival After Lung Cancer in patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis.
items.abstract: Despite the therapeutic benefits of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), concerns remain about their safety in patients with malignancy. Among patients with RA, we evaluated DMARD treatment patterns after lung cancer diagnosis and their association with survival. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Veterans Affairs (VA) Corporate Data Warehouse (2002-2022). Among patients with RA, incident lung cancers were identified from VA Oncology data. Information on comorbidities, smoking history, cancer stage at diagnosis, and histology were collected. DMARD exposure (none, conventional synthetic DMARDs [csDMARDs] only, and biologic or targeted synthetic DMARDs [b/tsDMARDs] (with or without csDMARDs)) were assessed at landmark points, during the first 3-months and 12-months, after cancer diagnosis. Associations between DMARD class and mortality were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted with energy balancing weights to balance demographic, RA-related, comorbidity, and cancer-related covariates across exposure groups. Among 1,651 patients with RA and lung cancer, 1,334 survived beyond 3 months and were included in the primary landmark analysis. DMARD exposure groups included no DMARD use in 498 patients (37.3%), csDMARD use in 643 (48.2%), and b/ts/combination DMARD use in 193 (14.5%). In adjusted analyses, neither csDMARDs nor b/ts/combination DMARDs were significantly associated with all-cause mortality or lung cancer-specific mortality at 3 years. Similar associations were observed in the 12-month landmark analysis. In U.S. Veterans with RA and lung cancer, DMARD use during the first year following cancer diagnosis was not associated with an increased 3-year mortality.

items.title: Acute Exacerbation of Interstitial Lung Disease Triggered by Chickenpox Pneumonia in Rheumatoid Arthritis: The Critical Role of Vaccination in Immunocompromised Patients.
items.abstract: A 67-year-old male with rheumatoid arthritis complicated by interstitial lung disease (ILD) was admitted to our hospital's intensive care unit due to acute respiratory distress syndrome, suggestive for acute exacerbation of ILD (AE-ILD). A few days before, he started a new therapy with a TNF-α inhibitor for his arthritis and had been exposed to chickenpox. Being unvaccinated, he contracted the infection, presenting with a diffuse vesicular rash and pneumonia. Despite the immediate initiation of acyclovir, his respiratory status deteriorated, requiring mechanical ventilation. Since both the viral infection and the TNF-α inhibitor were suspected triggers for AE-ILD, management focused on high-dose glucocorticoids and intravenous immunoglobulins, while further immunosuppressants were avoided due to the active infection. The patient's condition improved significantly, leading to discharge after 1 month. At follow-up, he had returned to his baseline functional status.

items.title: Interpreting immunoglobulin A evidence for the mucosal origins of rheumatoid arthritis autoimmunity.
items.abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) links barrier immunity, preclinical autoimmunity, and inflammatory effector pathways in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but these associations support different biological and clinical claims. This critical narrative review synthesizes selected human, structural, cellular, and animal studies through six dimensions: molecular identity, compartmental enrichment, local synthesis, clonal continuity, temporal order, and perturbation. Evidence coverage is distinguished from study credibility. Three judgments organize the synthesis. First, secretory component (SC)-associated anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA) signals require isotype resolution: early-RA depletion experiments implicate IgM, and SC association does not by itself locate initial activation. Second, IgA1-associated progression and stronger IgA2-mediated macrophage activation suggest that predictive and effector features may differ, but comparisons across designs do not establish subclass-specific clinical roles. Third, absence of detectable autoantibodies in the tested intestinal secretions constrains luminal output in the sampled RA populations; disease stage, treatment, and antibody-specific analytical sensitivity limit extrapolation to disease initiation. Antibody assembly and longitudinal clonal relationships provide complementary information without automatically establishing anatomical origin. Clinically, SC-ACPA may enrich risk among symptomatic IgG ACPA-positive individuals, including an RF-negative subgroup. Additional diagnostic or prognostic information from IgA-RF and IgA-ACPA is assay- and decision-dependent, and current evidence does not establish IgA-guided treatment selection. A clinical schematic separates target populations, observed associations, and proposed actions requiring validation. The framework connects each interpretation to its supporting observation, limitations, and next discriminating study.

items.title: Integrated proteomic, genetic, and machine-learning analyses reveal a CXCL11-centered inflammatory signature associated with systemic activity in Sjögren's disease.
items.abstract: Sjögren's disease (SjD) exhibits substantial clinical heterogeneity, and molecular biomarkers for systemic activity stratification remain limited. This study aimed to identify inflammatory protein signatures associated with systemic activity in SjD and evaluate their potential value for disease stratification and dynamic monitoring. A multi-stage biomarker discovery and validation framework integrating Olink targeted proteomics, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), clinical correlation analysis, machine-learning-based feature selection, Mendelian randomization (MR), and longitudinal assessment was established. Plasma inflammatory proteins were profiled using the Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel in the discovery cohort, and differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were identified. Candidate proteins were subsequently validated by ELISA in an independent cohort and evaluated for associations with clinical and immunological indices. LASSO, support vector machine-recursive feature elimination (SVM-RFE), and Random Forest algorithms were applied to identify core protein features. MR analysis was performed to assess the potential genetic relevance of prioritized inflammatory proteins to SjD susceptibility. Longitudinal changes in candidate biomarkers were further evaluated over a 24-week follow-up period. Olink proteomic profiling identified DEPs associated with systemic disease activity, with enrichment analyses highlighting cytokine-cytokine receptor interactions and chemokine signaling. ELISA validation confirmed differential expression of candidate inflammatory proteins between higher systemic activity (HSA) and low systemic activity (LSA) patients, and several proteins showed significant correlations with ESSDAI and immunological indices, including ESR, IgG, and RF. Machine-learning analyses consistently prioritized CXCL10 and CXCL11 as core protein features distinguishing HSA from LSA patients. MR analysis further provided genetic evidence supporting the potential relevance of CXCL11 to SjD susceptibility. During the 24-week longitudinal follow-up, plasma CXCL11 levels demonstrated dynamic changes and were significantly associated with changes in systemic activity-related parameters. This study identifies a CXCL11-centered inflammatory signature associated with systemic activity in SjD. By integrating targeted proteomics, machine learning, genetic evidence, and longitudinal validation, our findings highlight CXCL11 as a promising candidate biomarker for molecular stratification and dynamic monitoring of systemic inflammation in SjD.

items.title: Latent transitions of ego depletion during pharmacological therapy in newly diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis patients: implications for self-management behaviors.
items.abstract: To delineate latent transition patterns of ego depletion during csDMARD induction in newly diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and their association with self-management in this observational cohort. In this single-centre cohort, 255 newly diagnosed RA patients were enrolled and 230 completed assessments at baseline (T0), 3 (T1) and 6 months (T2). Ego depletion (SEDS) and self-management (RASMS) were evaluated. Latent profile analysis was conducted at each occasion and latent transition analysis modelled T1 → T2 transitions. Classification uncertainty was propagated with the Bolck-Croon-Hagenaars three-step method, and modal assignment served as a sensitivity analysis. Associations with T2 self-management were estimated with lagged models adjusted for the baseline score and for time-varying treatment and disease-activity covariates. Two latent classes were identified at T0 (low depletion 58.0%, moderate 42.0%) and three at T1 and T2 (low 25.2% and 32.2%, moderate 47.0% and 45.2%, high 27.8% and 22.6%). Entropy was 0.873-0.892; average posterior probabilities were 0.897-0.938, with classification error of 9.7% at T1 and 8.7% at T2. From T1 to T2 the moderate class was the most stable (88.89%) and the high class the least stable (65.63%); 13.9% of patients moved to a lower and 4.3% to a higher depletion class. Three transition cells contained 2-4 participants and were pooled. The T1 high depletion class was associated with a lower T2 total self-management score ( β  = -14.32, 95% CI: -17.86 to -10.78, P  < 0.001). Stable high depletion was associated with low-level self-management (OR = 4.106, 95% CI: 1.724-9.778) and poor medication adherence (OR = 4.482, 95% CI: 1.926-10.432); exposure and outcome were concurrent, so these are not temporal predictions. In this exploratory, single-centre cohort, ego depletion was heterogeneous and partly reversible during csDMARD induction. Persistent high depletion was associated with poorer self-management and medication adherence, but the observational and partly concurrent design precludes causal inference. Because only the T1-T2 interval was modelled, we cannot conclude that 3-6 months is uniquely a critical intervention window. External validation and intervention trials are required before targeted monitoring or psychological empowerment can be recommended.

items.title: Case Report: Central diabetes insipidus 15 years after a clinical diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
items.abstract: Pituitary involvement occurs in approximately 1% of patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), and arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D; central diabetes insipidus) is a frequent endocrine manifestation. AVP-D may be masked by other causes of polyuria. A 35-year-old woman with a 15-year history of a clinical diagnosis of GPA receiving immunosuppression was admitted with 2 months of anorexia. Appetite loss preceded a recent zoledronic acid infusion, after which further worsening was reported. Hypernatremia (peak: 157.1 mmol/L) was ascribed to poor intake, and polyuria was confounded by diabetes mellitus and suspected urinary infection. The admission urine specific gravity of 1.008 lay within the reference range yet was inappropriate for the concurrent hypernatremia; after rehydration, glycemic control, and antibiotics, hypotonic polyuria persisted. Plasma and urine osmolality were 295 and 70 mOsm/kg before desmopressin, and urine output fell markedly after oral desmopressin, supporting AVP-D. During a monitored oral desmopressin trial, 4-h urine output fell by 77.1% relative to the mean for the same interval on the preceding two observation days. Low free thyroxine with nonelevated TSH suggested possible central hypothyroidism. ANCA tests were negative in 2023 and 2026; results from the initial diagnosis were unavailable. Unenhanced sellar MRI showed a bulky pituitary containing a 7.6 mm × 6.1 mm lesion. Multidisciplinary review favored GPA-related posterior pituitary enlargement. The cause remained uncertain without histological confirmation or contrast-enhanced follow-up MRI, and histiocytic disorders could not be excluded. At telephone follow-up, the patient reported symptom control with desmopressin 0.1 mg twice daily. AVP-D can be masked by competing explanations for hypernatremia and polyuria. A specific gravity within the reference range does not exclude AVP-D when hypernatremia coexists. Attribution of the sellar lesion requires further investigation.

items.title: ANCA-Negative Pauci-Immune Crescentic Glomerulonephritis With Atypical Endothelial Injury in a Patient With Long-Standing Rheumatoid Arthritis.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic inflammatory disorder that may be complicated by diverse extra-articular manifestations, including renal involvement. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV) is an important cause of crescentic glomerulonephritis; however, ANCA-negative pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis in patients with RA is uncommon and diagnostically challenging. We herein report a case of ANCA-negative pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with atypical endothelial injury, clinically compatible with renal-limited AAV in a 70-year-old Japanese woman with long-standing RA. The patient had been treated with methotrexate and iguratimod, and abatacept was subsequently introduced for worsening joint symptoms. Although her articular manifestations improved, renal function began to decline 3 months after abatacept initiation. Laboratory tests showed renal dysfunction accompanied by hematuria and mild proteinuria, whereas serum MPO-ANCA and PR3-ANCA were negative. Kidney biopsy revealed crescentic glomerulonephritis with pauci-immune features, accompanied by prominent endocapillary hypercellularity and glomerular endothelial injury. The renal lesion was considered clinically compatible with ANCA-negative renal-limited AAV. Immunosuppressive therapy, including steroid pulse therapy, rituximab and avacopan, was initiated, leading to improvement in renal function and systemic inflammation. This case highlights the importance of kidney biopsy and careful clinicopathological assessment in patients with RA who develop unexplained renal impairment. Even in the absence of MPO-ANCA or PR3-ANCA, ANCA-negative pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis clinically compatible with renal-limited AAV should be considered, even when atypical endothelial injury is present.

items.title: 3-Hydroxy-3-Methylglutaryl-Coenzyme A Reductase Antibody-Positive Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy With Transaminitis and Nonspecific Liver Biopsy Findings in a Statin-Naive Patient.
items.abstract: Anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (anti-HMGCR) immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) causes proximal weakness and marked creatine kinase (CK) elevation. Serum aminotransferases may also increase with muscle injury and be mistaken for primary liver disease. We describe a 64-year-old man without statin exposure who developed five months of progressive proximal weakness and weight loss. CK and aminotransferases were markedly elevated, and anti-HMGCR antibodies were strongly positive. Hepatitis and autoimmune liver testing were unrevealing; liver biopsy showed mild nonspecific changes. Pulse methylprednisolone, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and a prednisone taper produced early functional improvement. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) normalized by approximately 6 months and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) by approximately 13 months, whereas CK first returned to its reference interval at approximately 18 months and remained normal at approximately 21 months. The clinical phenotype, severe hyperCKemia, anti-HMGCR seropositivity, magnetic resonance imaging findings, and longitudinal biochemical response favored a major skeletal muscle contribution to the aminotransferase elevation, although a concurrent mild hepatic process could not be definitively excluded; the biopsy did not demonstrate anti-HMGCR-mediated hepatic injury. Early CK measurement in patients with proximal weakness and transaminitis can clarify the source, while liver evaluation remains appropriate when supported by cholestatic markers, synthetic dysfunction, imaging, or histology.

items.title: Spondyloarthritis Following Recurrent Upper Respiratory Symptoms: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Reactive arthritis (ReA) and axial spondyloarthritis (axial SpA) share clinical features, including enthesitis and sacroiliitis. We report a 25-year-old man with spondyloarthritis (SpA) who exhibited features of both conditions. The patient had recurrent episodes of cough, sore throat, and fever of 37-39°C, each lasting approximately one week and separated by symptom-free intervals of approximately one week; approximately one week after the first episode developed low back pain and pain at the bilateral Achilles tendon and plantar fascia insertions. The back pain worsened at rest and upon waking and improved with exercise. C-reactive protein was 3.26 mg/dL; HLA-B27 was negative. Blood cultures, urine nucleic acid amplification tests for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae , and an interferon-gamma release assay were negative. Plain radiographs of the sacroiliac joints showed no definite structural abnormalities, whereas magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated bilateral high-signal lesions suggestive of bone marrow edema. SpA was diagnosed. Celecoxib 400 mg/day resolved the fever, back pain, and enthesitis within two weeks, and C-reactive protein decreased to 0.48 mg/dL. At nine months after the initiation of celecoxib, C-reactive protein was 0.13 mg/dL, sacroiliac joint radiographs showed no radiographic sacroiliitis, and the patient remained in remission. This case showed features suggestive of ReA, namely enthesitis following cold-like symptoms, together with features of axial SpA, namely inflammatory back pain and sacroiliac joint inflammation on MRI without radiographic sacroiliitis, consistent with non-radiographic axial SpA. Axial SpA should be considered when inflammatory back pain accompanies enthesitis after infectious symptoms. Sacroiliac joint MRI may detect inflammation before structural changes appear on plain radiography.

items.title: A Case of Legionella Disease Mimicking Dermatomyositis.
items.abstract: Legionella disease is a severe form of pneumonia that can present with rare extrapulmonary manifestations, potentially leading to diagnostic confusion. We report a 61-year-old man with alcohol dependence and heavy smoking who presented with severe pneumonia and systemic erythema, including seborrheic dermatitis-like erythema on the face, erythematous rashes spreading across the trunk, and livedo reticularis on the lower limbs. Laboratory findings showed markedly elevated ferritin, and computed tomography revealed widespread infiltrates and ground-glass opacities. Although empiric antibiotics were initiated, the presence of atypical cutaneous findings and progressive pulmonary lesions raised suspicion for autoimmune-associated organizing pneumonia, and prednisolone was initiated. The nonspecific cutaneous manifestations raised suspicion for dermatomyositis, but no pathognomonic rashes, such as Gottron papules or heliotrope rash, were observed, prompting further investigation for infection before escalating immunosuppression. A urinary antigen test subsequently confirmed Legionella pneumophila . The patient recovered fully after treatment with levofloxacin. This case highlights that Legionella disease can present with pulmonary and nonspecific cutaneous manifestations that may raise suspicion for dermatomyositis. Clinicians should consider Legionella infection in patients with severe pneumonia and atypical extrapulmonary manifestations, particularly those with relevant risk factors.
